title: The Boasting of the Gospel and the Conscience
english: Regarding the previous reproach to them, he does not reproach alone, and now in reconciling he does not write alone, but by the reception of holy Timothy he shows the matter to be reliable. And there indeed he showed that through which it was necessary for the Father, saying through the will of God (2 Cor 1:1).

Because in the former letter he did not reproach alone, and now in comforting he does not write alone, but by the reception of holy Timothy he shows the matter reliable (2 Cor 1:1–2). And because he says from God our Father, it is to be understood that regarding the begotten, he is called both God and Father, but regarding the Son only Father; for Christ, being the God of me and the God of you in the flesh, was saying so.

This glory which he glorifies and by names he names God, already foretells that of reconciliation (2 Cor 1:3). Father of mercies and God of all comfort; for regarding the begotten he is called both God and Father, but regarding the Son only he is confessed as Father. He begins intimately with those being afflicted from the mercies of God and comfort, showing to them good hopes; for if God is the Father of mercies, he would have comforted those being persecuted and afflicted through him.
Comforting, God does not make the comfort a small thing (2 Cor 1:4). He pre-announces these things, because it was going to call back the one condemned through sin by means of comfort.

Our affliction becomes comfort to you; for if the apostles are afflicted, much more the others (2 Cor 1:6). Or he also says this: if even we are being afflicted by men for the sake of your salvation, we suffer this, because we preach Christ to you. If we receive comfort from God through you, so that we may be sufficient for your exhortation, so as to urge you to suffer the same things which even we undergo.
I hope that undergoing the same things for me, similarly from God and from the comfort...
Not boasting, he recounts the tribulations that befell him in Asia (2 Cor 1:8), but rather encourages them toward endurance of the sufferings. Instead of [saying] so as to forbid us even to live.

It is said that the decision from judgment is a response (2 Cor 1:9). How much therefore [is] upon themselves: for we have had the decision of death (2 Cor 1:9), through which we are being disciplined not to trust in ourselves but in the saving God and those who forbid themselves [to trust in self].

He does not pray for those attacking [him] to flee as if they were lovers of the body, but so that [it] may be useful to the gifts given to him, so that through many persons of the now and through many of those coming, the preaching that saves them may be thanked; for having said [it], he demonstrated the teaching of those coming through many. And that [it] may be thanked on your behalf instead of the gift for which we ourselves have also received.

This is our boasting: that our conscience testifies to us that we preach rightly (2 Cor 1:12). And indeed he intends the wisdom of those from the outside to be merely natural, but now it is implied that he did not use speech according to the outsiders; in that, to take something from them, he did not have the cause of the preaching to be fleshly (2 Cor 1:13–14). We did not teach you other things, agreeing with you, apart from what we now send, but these things which even as you read, being unadorned: whence also you recognize that our word is as an ordinary man, but the power of God working toward faith (2 Cor 1:13–14).

Paul says boasting of himself in those things in which he was approved by preaching; but the boasting of the Corinthians themselves is in the day of Christ, as if they possessed glory in those things in which they received the preaching. I hope that you will come to know, since even now you have already partially come to know that in the day of the Lord we are your boasting, just as you are ours; for those who have preached in those things in which they were approved are venerable, but those who were zealous in those things in which they believed the preaching. Not for a fleshly reason did I consult/plan to come (2 Cor 1:17), but because of the...

title: Severianus on 2 Corinthians 2
english: God: the matter of deciding through God to come about is not a light thing. Having decided to come to you, I promised this to you not by rashness or lightness; for not according to the flesh do I decide, but spiritually. It is proper that one deciding concerning spiritual things should nowhere be false, so that his yes may be yes and his no, no.

Indeed, whether it is to come or not to come is not in me, but the setting forth in me (2 Kor 1:18). If, therefore, the proclamation had yes and no, my decision regarding my arrival to you would justly have yes and no; but if the word is true, then the whole decision is true. I believe to God that none of those things which we preached is a lie (2 Kor 1:19). For even the Son of God, our Lord Jesus, did not become a liar (2 Kor 1:19). Through Christ we send up the amen to God the Father, and the confirmation toward Christ we received through God; and through the one having sealed us, He demonstrated our belonging to God and our separation from the evil one (2 Kor 1:20–22). For even shepherds place their own seal upon the flocks, distinguishing them from the strangers. Having said 'earnest', He presented that we have received a small deposit of the knowledge, but the perfection is owed to us; for the earnest is a part of the whole.

Because there were many complaints against them, he did not want, having gone, to condemn them (2 Kor 1:23–24). The word is spoken incompletely; for he wants to say that I desired to come to you, but not as one who is lord and teacher of your faith. To stumble you among you, and to correct those stumbling among us, so that we might become fellow-workers of the joy according to God. To believe in you, and in us the correcting of those stumbling, so that we might become fellow-workers of the grace of God. And he says 'joy according to God'; for the apostle would not have joined in with them for a worldly joy. Having spoken of faith, he presented that they are left without works. Therefore, since they have faith as unfruitful and still incomplete, he says he is a fellow-worker to them.

Because of this I did not come, not so that I might not grieve you but myself, and so that I might not condemn anyone on account of what they are doing (2 Kor 2:1). You do not grieve me from those who are alike, and I you; for you grieve me from those from whom you sin, but I grieve you from those whom I strike (2 Kor 2:2). But rejoice...

He appears to be feeling sorrow—for he who has not been grieved clearly shows that he did not even take heed when rebuked (2 Kor 2:3). For even if I grieve you, I am doing a proper thing; cooperate toward my joy regarding your own benefit.

I wrote this, that sparing you, I did not come, so that at the end of this letter, where it lies, lest having come, God might humble me (2 Kor 2:4). And because of this I wrote, so that in gladness I might find you having been corrected, so that you might not grieve. Not looking to my own, but to yours I said this; for I know that if you see me rejoicing, you rejoice, and if you see me grieving, you grieve. I wrote these things so that if you wish for me to come to you, you might beforehand correct the faults.

Showing that he makes the same faults his own, he brought grief and tears, which he has love toward them (2 Kor 2:5). Having said, I wrote to you, not that you might simply be grieved, but that the joy according to God might take away the grief.

If anyone has grieved even him whom you love, he has not grieved me alone, but in part also you, so that I might not burden [you] by saying even Christ (2 Kor 2:6). And he fell silent from saying 'and Christ,' so that he might not burden [you] even by saying it.

He says 'reproof' is the condemnation from the many (2 Kor 2:7). To forgive him this (2 Kor 2:8). Obey me in condemning, obey me also in recalling him who has been condemned (2 Kor 2:9). Forgive him this, he says; for you know that of those which you forgive to this [man], I also desire to forgive (2 Kor 2:10). And because of this he shows that he wants them to think the same things about themselves by a disposition toward them.

He appears to have been grieved toward those in Troas, because they did not do much regarding Titus, nor did they hold him until his arrival, but as if they had become lawless concerning the faith, they departed (2 Kor 2:12-13). Thus, admonishing them as unworthy, he departed even though a door had been opened and no one was closing against the proclamation. Or indeed because of this he departed, as being able easily to correct the things there later upon arrival, as no one being there to hinder.

This is to the one proclaiming our insults and the circumstances through Christ (2 Kor 2:14). But he confesses a greater grace regarding those things through which he is made worthy to triumph through Christ. And he says these things also because of the Corinthians; for it was feared lest they might perhaps slay [him] because of the things...

title: The Law as Ministry of Death vs the Spirit as Ministry of Life
english: Enduring afflictions and falling away from salvation (2 Cor 2:15–16). The idolaters, being in death to the intelligible due to the ignorance and hardness existing in them, fall a second time into death because they do not receive the evangelical preaching; but those who, having come to the beginnings of the knowledge of God through the legal instruction, have perhaps become somewhat in life, yet if they believe in Christ, they receive the fragrance of the knowledge of the Father from life unto life.

Shortly after, he interprets this passage differently. Such things are established by Christ being a fragrance, not of those happening by chance but of those serving God sincerely. And as he does not say these things about himself as a burden, but from which he proceeds, he says, 'for we are not as many as many are,' and he demonstrated himself (2 Cor 2:17).

He says that to peddle the word means to mingle with circumcision and keep Sabbaths, or to think that some consider piety to be a profit. I say, however, that he speaks from sincerity, and says that this very thing is from God, and not from a private power. He also says another thought, that because of this it is from sincerity, since we speak from God, not playing with things but preaching the revelation of God. He says this because there were also false apostles who considered the word concerning piety to be a profit. Then he proceeds from sincerity, instead of 'we do not play with things,' he says, 'but we preach the revelation from God, not peddling the word of God.' The word of God is peddled by mingling with circumcision and the Sabbath and in thinking that piety is a profit.

From here he wants to show how much the law of grace leaves behind, so that none of those from the circumcision, while hypocritically facing those from the Gentiles, might lead them into the observance of the requirement of Moses and the prophets (2 Cor 3:1). This is your faith and your life, becoming a letter to all and a recognition of our preaching (2 Cor 3:2–3). Because of saying 'stony tablets' and 'fleshy hearts,' he shows the superiority of grace over the law, in that the tablet of the soulless heart is greater. He also shows how much the grace of the Spirit remains superior to the law and the ministry of the prophets' preaching.

Higher than the apostles, from themselves rather than from one another (2 Cor 3:5). The letter says the law, but the Spirit says grace (2 Cor 3:6); for the law, while commanding, does not help, but is heavy and kills through punishment those unable to fulfill it, whereas the Spirit makes one clean from sin and provides gifts, clearly leading toward life (2 Cor 3:6). And indeed the glory did not come on tablets but on the face of Moses, as he himself says (2 Cor 3:7–9), because of the glory of his face which was fading (2 Cor 3:7–9).

But not wishing to speak against the prophet Moses, he calls the law Moses, and in this way makes the statement, showing the grace given to Moses to be lesser than the apostolic grace. If he calls the ministry of death—Moses calls it a ministry of death, calling the law death, because it brought forth death through disobedience—yet the law is not slandered by this; for even the apostles are called a stench of death unto death. He calls the apostles a ministry of the Spirit, and Moses a ministry of death. But sparing Moses, he remembers the tablets; Moses brought down tablets from the mountain, but the apostles, having been sent with the Spirit, brought it to the world.

And indeed the glory did not come on tablets but on the face of Moses. And wishing to speak here also regarding Moses, he makes Moses evident through the law. He calls the law itself a minister of death, because the law kills those not fulfilling it. And he does not say this as slandering him, for he also said the apostles are a stench of death because of those not obeying the proclamation. The stench of death is the threat of Gehenna bringing eternal death upon the unbelievers, and the stench of life is the proclamation of the kingdom sending those following the teaching into eternal life. The stench is a forerunner of the reality.

He calls Moses a minister of condemnation and death—for he condemned in the law those not obeying—and the apostles a minister of the Spirit; for Moses brought down the law, but the apostles conveyed the Spirit to the world. The letter of the law, which was glorified, has not been glorified when examined against the surpassing glory of the Spirit (2 Cor 3:10). No one could say that it was glorified in this word.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Transformation from Law to Spirit
english: Concerning the comparison with the superior one. 2 Cor 3:11 showed that it was necessary to cease and to be idle regarding the law, but the grace of the Spirit, having been opposed to the law, remains. 2 Cor 3:12–14 Having therefore such a hope. The hope that is seen is not a hope; but he showed that the grace remains, even after the resurrection, receiving the additions, toward the inability of the sons of Israel to gaze intently until the end of the one being made void; for just as they were not able to attend to the glory... so they were not able even to the end of the law, that is, that the law shall be ceased. He says immediately: until today they have a veil. The end of the law is when the veil is taken away and they behold the glory of the Spirit, because in Christ it is made void, that is, it is through the faith into him.

What kind of hope? That the grace of the Spirit is not made void like the law, but remains even after the resurrection. We, because of the blessed hope of the grace of the Spirit remaining, teach with boldness, and we do not imitate the commands of Moses, who through the veil upon the face signaled that the Jews are not able to gaze intently and realize that the law shall receive an end and shall be idle. The veil remains showing no appearance, that the law is made void upon the coming of Christ. 2 Cor 3:15–16 Just as Moses, while speaking to the Jews, had the veil, but returning to the Lord it is taken away, and now the Jews, after reading the law and returning the book, carry the veil as if Moses had returned to the Lord. If therefore, having turned away, you come to the Spirit, your veil is taken away just as Moses' was being taken away when returning to the Lord. 2 Cor 3:17 The one made worthy of the Spirit of the Lord, this one was freed from the condemnation of the law; for through the Spirit the gifts are being worked. And the gift is toward the worthy ones. 2 Cor 3:18 We, he says, the apostles, are seen by men with an unveiled face; but having said this, we all demonstrate the common benefit of the Spirit. And for Moses the glory was not approaching the Israelites, but for us the glory of God is approaching; for having established ourselves on faith, we reflect the glory of God, that is, we see and are being changed as into...

We are being transformed from legal knowledge into spiritual grace, moving from the glory of the Spirit working in us toward the glory of adoption. This is made clear by the Lord Spirit, not the Son of God. Just as one sees in that mirror, and another receives the reflection of the one seeing, so it is with the Spirit; for those reflecting the glory of Christ carry a certain likeness from that glory into glory, that is, they receive and take upon themselves the glory of the spiritual image.

We are being transformed from legal knowledge into spiritual grace, and from the glory not of the law but of the Spirit, into the glory of adoption; for we come to adoption through a washing. He says 'of grace', not 'of the law'; for through the abundance of grace we endure tribulations. The shameful and the base things are hidden, which those practicing strive to hide because of shame; for the base things do not partake of boldness, but wander in darkness. Even if the gospel is covered, it is covered to the unbelieving, not as the glory of Moses' face was covered from all Israel in the law (2 Cor 4:3).

If the god of this age is said to be associated with reading, it follows that he blinded them. But if God blinded, it was supernaturally, as God gave them a spirit of stupor, eyes that do not see, and 'I hardened the heart of Pharaoh' (Exodus 10:27) according to the spoken word. Just as it was said of a ruler, not that he is naturally a ruler, but that those deceived showed him to be their ruler by obeying him, so also the god of this age has been forbidden, not as being truly God, but because of what the nations say and think, being called God, just as the belly is called the god of gluttons.

He says, 'If we had preached ourselves, it would be possible to suppose that we are deceiving with the word' (2 Cor 4:5); but if Jesus Christ and his glory, there is no deceit in the preaching according to the...

title: The Weight of Glory and the Two Dwellings
english: It is said: he who seeks his own glory is not true, but he who seeks the glory of the one who sent him, he is true. If we were proclaiming ourselves, it would be suspected that we are deceiving with the word, but if we proclaim Christ and his glory, there is no deception in the preaching.

In the face of Jesus Christ (2 Cor 4:6), instead of 'through Jesus Christ', through him. Toward the illumination of knowledge, that the knowledge was not found by reasoning, but was revealed through revelation. Instead of 'through Jesus Christ' it shone in our hearts, and the knowledge was not found by reasoning, but was made known through revelation and illumination; for no man could ever reach this, having been clothed in flesh (2 Cor 4:7–9).

Through these and the following, he shows that God does not allow to be tested beyond what we are able. For even if we are being afflicted by those who persecute, yet we are not so distressed as to have no escape or recourse anywhere; for God widens the way for those afflicted through piety, whence also David says: 'In affliction you widened me' (2 Cor 4:10).

We always carry the death, always risking because, being partakers of the sufferings of Christ, we are [at risk] (2 Cor 4:11). The Lord was delivered unto death for us, but we for ourselves through Jesus, so that we might become partakers of his life (2 Cor 4:12).

Because of the preaching the apostles were risking, but they proclaimed so that the believing ones might live, and this is the life in you (2 Cor 4:13). Since, he says, there is a spirit of slavery in the law, but a spirit of adoption in the grace. And he said that we have the same spirit which David also had; the same spirit added the faith, not of the legal slavery. Having, he says, the same spirit as David who spoke according to faith, just as he said: 'I believed, therefore I spoke' (Psalm 116:5). Then, having said 'the spirit added the faith', for this is common to new and old only, since in the law there was a spirit of slavery, but in the grace a spirit of adoption.

If deaths and dangers and temptations follow (2 Cor 4:17–18), how is the affliction lighter? How is it being spent away? For the temptations remained with him and were driving him into old age. How then is the affliction of the saints light? Or is it evident that, being weighed against the glory of the coming age and against the prepared good things for the righteous, even the heaviest temptations appear light to me? And the afflictions are not merely light, but excessive, yet these afflictions fall far short of the greatness of the glory; for the great thing is a body and is heavy. Or he said 'weight' by way of a metaphor of the scales; for the glory, being weighed against the afflictions, is found to be most heavy of all. And he says 'spent away' regarding the temporal; for even if the crushing is long and causes grief, it appears temporal as compared to the infinite glory.

A dwelling, a tent; not the tent but the dwelling (2 Cor 5:1–2); for the dwelling here ceases, but the tent rises up. And he said 'dwelling' for the conduct, both the mortal and the expected. Furthermore, he shows that he calls the corruption and the incorruption 'dwellings'. He says 'dwelling, tent' regarding the body, which, he says, even if it should be corrupted in temptations and dangers through Christ, we shall lay it aside as a corruptible dwelling among the last of things made by hands. But we shall find in the heavens another dwelling, which God provides, incorruptible and not made by hands. Through these things, he shows both the mortal conduct and the immortal. Through the 'putting on', he shows that the corruptible flesh rises up and puts on the immortal; for the 'putting on' is said in reference to another garment. And he says 'two dwellings', the mortal and the expected; and 'two habitations', the corruption and the incorruption, because we are being laid aside from the one and are putting on the other. And he calls the one from heaven 'habitation'—the incorruption from the heavens—since it is not made by hands but is a gift of God. All indeed are righteous and unrighteous (2 Cor 5:3)...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.
baehrens: PG Fragmenta in epistulam ii ad Corinthios u02-open

title: Death to the World and the New Creation
english: They are clothed in incorruption. But if anyone is handed over to punishment, he is no different from being naked (2 Cor 5:4). The following is intended: that which we want to be clothed with is incorruption, but not to strip off the body itself into corruption. Therefore also it has led to this: so that the mortal might be swallowed up by life (2 Cor 5:5). For this very purpose, it is evident, to become incorruptible (2 Cor 5:5).

Instead of being convinced that, while residing in the body, that is to say, still passing through this world in the flesh (2 Cor 5:6), we hope through faith toward God (2 Cor 5:7); for his appearance is not visible to us; but this we believe, that we shall depart to him, when we shall see him, insofar as it is possible to see God as a man (2 Cor 5:8). For Moses also saw bodily, and angels see as it is possible for them to see; for no one has ever seen God, and every creature of God leaves behind the sight (2 Cor 5:8).

If you are pleasing here, you will be even more pleasing there without contradiction, no longer struggling but having the security of being pleasing (2 Cor 5:9). And it enters into [the thought] that we walk through faith, not through sight, and concerning the economy of the God the Word to be spoken, since he himself was not among those who had seen the Lord in the flesh before the passion (2 Cor 5:10).

Those who please men and boast not through piety, it is evident they boast through the face of men; for the heart is observed by God (2 Cor 5:11). Boasting is called ecstasy (2 Cor 5:12). Let us boast so that he may be glorified; let us keep silence regarding boasting—which he says is to be prudent—in order that I may teach you not to boast (2 Cor 5:13). But ecstasy is called the one who, having to flee from boasting, is compelled to boast. The boasting regarding the state of affairs is called ecstasy; for boasting has gone out of bounds, while the prudent ones measure. Often, therefore, we are compelled to step out and boast, so that God may be glorified through us. But we strive to be prudent and to measure, so that I may also teach you not to boast. And he says ecstasy regarding the one who, having to speak, is compelled to boast, to come to this.
Desiring to be silent, we are compelled to boast, being compelled by the love of Christ, so that he might be glorified (2 Cor 5:14–15).

All have died; he speaks of the faithful as being dying to the world both through baptism and through life. And they no longer live for themselves; for even I, if I were living for myself, I would not have boasted, but since I live for Christ, through him I am silent if it would be for your benefit, and through him I boast, so that he might be glorified. Whether we are beside ourselves or we act with prudence for you, we do everything through the love of Christ (2 Cor 5:17). Since he who dies for some rescues those already judged from death, and insofar as we were dead regarding what concerns us, if one died for all, therefore all have died insofar as to the condemnation. But he speaks of the faithful, who through baptism were crucified to the world, no longer living for themselves but for Christ; for Christ, having died for all and having paid the common debt, made the world his debtor.

Thus we from now on know no one according to the flesh (2 Cor 5:16). Since circumcision is of the flesh, and this to eat and that not to eat, and the Sabbath, he says that we of the faithful know no one according to the flesh. But since it was expedient for the Lord to be circumcised and to keep the Sabbath, he says this opportunely, so that he might benefit those under the law. But now we do not yet... have known this; for he does not want us to live according to the law. This was said not only to crucify the desires, but also not even to obey the law any longer; for even if Christ was circumcised and became subject to the observances of the law—that is, even if we knew Christ according to the flesh—but now we no longer know him. For when he was among men, as a man he lived out his citizenship fulfilling the law by his life; but having died and having risen, incorruptible, he abolished the things of the law and showed the way of the heavenly citizenship. Therefore also those being baptized, as if dying to bodily citizenships, imitate the pure conduct in the heavens and join themselves according to the heart to God. If anyone lives in Christ and is baptized, this one is a new creation (2 Cor 5:17), no longer living according to the law but according to the new grace of the Spirit. For whether you say law or grace, all [flow] from...

title: Paul's exhortation and the Macedonian example
english: Of God; for we do not even say that the law is not from God, even if it reached its end. He says the proclamation is a ministry of reconciliation, through which believing ones shall be reconciled to God (2 Cor 5:18-19). Thus it must be understood: that God was reconciling the world to himself in Christ. Thus then it must be grasped: that God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself, which is to say through Christ (2 Cor 5:19).

Now we are ambassadors instead of Christ, entreating you by God through us (2 Cor 5:20). Then also he shows that he is grieved because of those keeping the law; for on account of Christ, he says, not on account of the law (2 Cor 5:20). And God entreats through us as through Christ, of whom we are ministers and servants (2 Cor 5:20).

He showed from here how he is grieved because of those striving who keep the law; for keeping the law, he says, we have become sinners (2 Cor 5:21). Christ has become sin, so that he might deliver us from sin (2 Cor 5:21). And God provided these things; receive the reconciliation, turning away from keeping the legalities (2 Cor 6:1).

It was permitted to the apostles not only to entreat but also to cooperate and suffer with them toward salvation, so that they might sincerely receive the grace from God (2 Cor 6:4). As an unbreakable foundation, endurance is pre-laid, which enduring, it is easy to face every trial (2 Cor 6:7).

The weapons of righteousness: the right hand to have the work of good things, and the left to abstain from the work of evil things, and through both of these righteousness is established; for it is clear that when one is absent, the other becomes idle (2 Cor 6:7). Through the glory, indeed, of those receiving the word and marveling at it, and through the dishonor of those insulting the believing ones; and the same word is also regarding the following (2 Cor 6:8).

Having said 'do not be compressed in us', he teaches this: instead of 'we do not compress you with the saving teaching, nor shall there be a lack from us'; for our heart has been widened and our mouth has been opened for teaching (2 Cor 6:11-13). And you therefore, as in a response, widen your own mind and receive the teaching; for your heart has not been enlarged in such a way as to receive the teachings from me. So that you are not compressed by yourselves, not being more [than we]...

And [they are] receptive. 2 Cor 7:9 'Receive us, saying, so that in nothing we may be harmed by us.' For if I kept silent, he says, and did not strike, you were not grieved; but if you were not grieved, you would have been harmed if you were not repenting. I rejoice, he says, over your afflictions, because they are not worldly but spiritual. And he remembers next the things happening to him through Christ in Asia. 2 Cor 7:12 And indeed because of this he wrote. But as it seems and as the outcome showed, not because of this I wrote, but so that your eagerness and your obedience might be shown; so that through another appearance, another was understood. 2 Kor 7:13 In this he has been refreshed, because they were obeying his teaching.

2 Kor 8:2 In which, he says, they are greatly afflicted being persecuted, in this they rejoice more, and their poverty according to the depth overflowed into the wealth of their generosity. And the apostle testifies to the Macedonians that being poor they became bountiful in well-doing, so that also the Corinthians might be stirred toward fruitfulness. 2 Kor 8:6 The eagerness of the Macedonians toward well-doing prompted us to entreat Titus to come to you, so that he might also prompt you toward fruitfulness. And because of this he also said this, since they had from him the grace of the teaching. 2 Kor 8:8 Through the others, he says, of the Macedonians.

2 Kor 8:18— This joining to the fact that we sent along the brother, whose praise is in the gospel, so that with much and vigorous well-doing from those of the Gentiles they might suffice to serve, being restrained and guarded, lest anyone should blame us as hindering the well-doing toward the saints. Before the Lord it is good to serve in well-doing, and before men not to be blamed and slandered in the vigor of the ministry. 2 Kor 10:2–6 Not as the soldiers of the world receive pay, so also we preach regarding receiving pay. And having readiness to avenge every disobedience, when your obedience is fulfilled. Because I knew that some are persuaded by speech and exhortation, I was not willing immediately to use the sword, as I consider against some, since they did not seem to be obeying by speech alone. First, however...

title: Defense of Apostolic Integrity and the Nature of Paul's Afflictions
english: I struck with the word, so that those being restored by it might correct themselves, and those disobedient to the word might be reproved, while those needing a separation by deeds [are identified].

Knowing that some are being persuaded even while hearing, I do not wish to use separation yet; rather, when those obeying appear, it may be shown who are being instructed by the word and who are in need of a turning back. Test accurately each one according to the worthiness of the face's conduct (2 Kor 10:7). This he sees regarding the apostles; for since it was destined to reprove those from circumcision, and they were putting forward Peter and James and John, be certain, he says, lest the status of faces might ever prevent you from perceiving the truth. We write these things not imitating those commending themselves—for this is not good (2 Kor 10:12)—for they do not perceive that they themselves measure themselves within themselves and are not able to compare themselves to another; for when compared to others they are nothing. We do not boast beyond our measure as if we were superior to greater things (2 Kor 10:14); for even unto you we came and proclaimed the word (2 Kor 10:15–16). They boast of their own labors regarding our things, but we do not, but according to law we boast of the rule and the measure allotted to us, hoping to evangelize even beyond you as your faith increases. And he says 'rule' to mean reaching as far as them (2 Kor 10:17). Even if we boast, it is not as if we were rectifying by our own wisdom, but by the grace of the Spirit (2 Kor 11:2). You died, he says, to the law, and have become another man, to the one risen from the dead. How then could a pure virgin have been previously married? But having been reborn through the bath of regeneration and having passed into another life, a pure virgin is justly so named. Faith in Christ and the brightness of the Spirit confirm the Christian life (2 Kor 11:4). If then you did not receive these things, you seek well those who still wish to live according to the law (2 Kor 11:10–12). Not reproaching the Corinthians, he says this, but reproving those who use the preaching as a matter of commerce. Therefore he says that I do not stop boasting.

He means that I have not made the preaching a commercial venture like those; for I neither received anything from you nor do I receive, not as one not loving you—for I do love—but so that I might cut off the pretext of the accusers, so that whether they boast falsely or truly, they may be revealed just as we also are revealed (2 Cor 12:2–5).

To show this a strong, immortal soul; for if he had known it was mortal, he would not have been wavering whether he saw the vision outside the body or in the body. And regarding the third heaven, he said the third of the expanse; for if he had ascended up to the three heavens, he certainly would have heard the unspeakable words there and not in Paradise. And let no one suppose Paradise to be above the heaven; for according to the east it is planted upon the earth in the place of Eden, whence also Adam was formed, as Moses recounts. And he speaks of persecutions as weaknesses, not a bodily passion as some suppose (2 Cor 12:7).

It is suspected by many as having a pain around the head, but the truth is he speaks of persecutions, since the temptations came from a diabolical energy. And he called the one serving the temptation to the devil a Satanic angel, from a transformation of the angels serving God. And that which was given according to the forgiveness of God should be understood as also regarding Job; for God does not give evil (2 Cor 12:9).

You have an apostolic grace; do not seek this and succeed even without temptations; for my power is perfected in persecutions and tribulations (2 Cor 12:13). If then you have nothing to accuse me of, that I, having desisted from seeking sustenance despite the need, received nothing from you, in which even if you think I have sinned, forgive me and grant me grace for this injustice which you think is being done by me (2 Cor 12:14).

This testifies to them regarding the second and third time to be toward them because of the preaching (2 Cor 13:4). Just as Christ was said to have become sin and a curse, being neither sin nor a curse, but he took upon himself our evils so that we might be delivered from them; so also now, he is said to have been crucified not from his own weakness, but from that which he received on our behalf, the dispensations on our behalf.
